body:
The four forces of flight

An aircraft is a vehicle designed to travel through the air. Military aircraft differ in their tasks, but their flight depends on the same basic physical principles: forces, motion, pressure and energy.

Four principal forces act on a fixed-wing aircraft in flight:

  • Lift: The aerodynamic force produced mainly by the wings, acting perpendicular to the direction of airflow.
  • Weight: The force of gravity acting towards the Earth.
  • Thrust: The force produced by engines or propellers that drives the aircraft forward.
  • Drag: Air resistance that opposes the aircraft's movement through the air.

In steady, level flight at constant speed, lift approximately balances weight, while thrust balances drag. To climb, descend, turn or change speed, the aircraft changes the magnitude or direction of these forces.

A fixed-wing aircraft produces lift because its wings interact with moving air. The wing changes the airflow, creating an aerodynamic force. Pressure differences around the wing and the downward deflection of air are related explanations of lift; neither should be treated as an entirely separate force.

For ordinary fixed-wing aircraft, sufficient airflow over the wings is necessary to maintain lift. This is why conventional aeroplanes generally accelerate along a runway before take-off. Some specially designed aircraft can take off or land vertically, but that is not the normal operating method of fixed-wing transports or fighters.

Aircraft propulsion

Jet engines

A jet engine takes in air, compresses it, adds energy through fuel combustion and expels gases to produce thrust. Jet-powered fighters are useful where high speed and rapid response are important. A turbofan is a common type of jet engine that uses a fan as well as the engine's exhaust to produce thrust.

Propeller-driven aircraft

A propeller acts as a rotating aerodynamic device that pushes air backwards and produces forward thrust. A turboprop aircraft uses a gas turbine to drive its propeller. Turboprops are widely used for transport duties where suitable operating speed, fuel efficiency and performance from shorter airstrips are valuable.

Helicopters

A helicopter obtains most of its lift from rotating blades called the main rotor. Because these blades move through the air even when the helicopter has little forward speed, a helicopter can hover, take off vertically and land in comparatively small spaces.

A conventional single-main-rotor helicopter also needs a means to control the turning tendency created by the main rotor, commonly a tail rotor. Other helicopter designs use different rotor arrangements to achieve the same basic purpose.

Military aircraft by role

Aircraft typeMain purposeCharacteristic
FighterAir combat and air defenceHigh manoeuvrability and combat systems
Multirole fighterAir combat and attacks on surface targetsCan perform more than one combat role
Transport aircraftMovement of personnel, cargo and suppliesCargo capacity and logistical flexibility
HelicopterVertical-lift transport, rescue, reconnaissance or combatHovering and vertical take-off and landing
Maritime patrol aircraftSurveillance over the seaLong-range observation and specialised sensors

These are functional categories rather than completely separate technologies. A helicopter may carry troops or conduct reconnaissance. A fighter may also undertake surveillance. An aircraft's designation should therefore be understood together with its actual role.

Prelims focus

  • The four principal forces of flight are lift, weight, thrust and drag.
  • A turboprop uses a turbine engine to drive a propeller; it is not the same as a pure jet-powered fighter.
  • Helicopters generate lift mainly through rotating rotor blades and can hover.
  • A transport aircraft primarily provides logistical mobility rather than air combat.
  • Trap: Lift does not act in the same direction as thrust, and helicopters do not need a conventional runway for vertical take-off.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 11, 'Force and Pressure', and Ch. 12, 'Friction'; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Ch. 8, 'Motion', and Ch. 9, 'Force and Laws of Motion'; NASA Glenn Research Center, 'Four Forces on an Airplane' and 'Airplane Cruise – Balanced Forces', consulted 14 November 2026.]

body:
Why different aircraft are required

A country's air force needs aircraft for different purposes. Fighter aircraft protect airspace and perform combat missions. Transport aircraft move personnel and equipment. Helicopters operate where vertical lift, hovering or access to difficult terrain is important. These requirements explain why a military fleet contains several aircraft types rather than a single universal model.

Tejas: India's Light Combat Aircraft

Tejas is an indigenous Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) developed for the Indian Air Force. It is a lightweight, multirole fighter capable of air defence and selected strike and reconnaissance missions. The Aeronautical Development Agency has led the design and development programme, while Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) manufactures the aircraft.

Tejas uses a jet engine and a modern flight-control system. Its fly-by-wire system interprets pilot control inputs electronically and commands the aircraft's control surfaces. Fly-by-wire describes a method of flight control; it does not mean that the aircraft flies without a pilot.

The first Tejas squadron, No. 45 Squadron of the Indian Air Force, was formed on 1 July 2016. The Tejas Mk 1 programme achieved formal Final Operational Clearance on 20 February 2019. Operational clearance concerns an aircraft configuration and its approved capabilities; it should not be confused with the date of the aircraft's first flight or the formation of its first squadron.

C-295: Military transport and Gujarat's aerospace industry

The Airbus C-295 is a twin-turboprop tactical transport aircraft. It can move troops, supplies and other cargo and is suitable for operations from relatively short or less-developed airstrips. Its rear cargo ramp helps the movement of cargo and personnel. The aircraft is intended to replace the Indian Air Force's older Avro transport fleet.

India signed a contract for 56 C-295 aircraft in September 2021. The programme provides for 16 aircraft from Spain in fly-away condition and 40 aircraft to be manufactured and assembled in India through Tata Advanced Systems Limited in partnership with Airbus.

The Tata Aircraft Complex at Vadodara, Gujarat, was inaugurated on 28 October 2024. It was established as India's first private-sector final assembly line for military aircraft. The first India-made C-295 successfully completed its maiden test flight at Vadodara on 10 June 2026, as announced by the Indian Air Force and Airbus. A test flight establishes a flight-testing milestone; it does not, by itself, establish delivery or operational induction.

Prachand: India's Light Combat Helicopter

Prachand is India's indigenously designed and developed Light Combat Helicopter (LCH), produced by HAL. Unlike the C-295, its principal purpose is combat support rather than cargo transport. A helicopter's ability to hover and operate in difficult terrain is particularly useful in mountainous regions.

On 28 March 2025, the Ministry of Defence signed contracts for the supply of 156 Prachand helicopters: 66 for the Indian Air Force and 90 for the Indian Army. These figures describe the contracts signed on that date; they must not be interpreted as the number delivered or inducted on that date.

Other aircraft and role distinctions

The Indian Air Force also operates fighters such as the Su-30MKI and Rafale. Their primary classification is combat aircraft. The Navy uses maritime patrol aircraft such as the P-8I for surveillance over the sea, a role distinct from transporting routine cargo.

Indian examplePlatform categoryPrincipal association
TejasLight multirole fighterAir defence and combat missions
C-295Tactical transport aircraftMovement of personnel and cargo
PrachandLight combat helicopterRotary-wing combat support
P-8IMaritime patrol aircraftMaritime surveillance and anti-submarine duties

Prelims focus

  • Tejas is an indigenous Light Combat Aircraft; its first IAF squadron was formed on 1 July 2016.
  • Tejas Mk 1 received formal Final Operational Clearance on 20 February 2019.
  • The C-295 programme covers 56 aircraft: 16 from Spain and 40 to be produced in India.
  • The C-295 final assembly complex at Vadodara was inaugurated on 28 October 2024.
  • The first India-made C-295 completed its maiden test flight on 10 June 2026.
  • The 28 March 2025 Prachand contracts cover 156 helicopters: 66 for the IAF and 90 for the Army. Trap: A contract, test flight and operational induction are different milestones.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Tejas inducted into No 45 Squadron of Indian Air Force', 1 July 2016; 'Final Operational Clearance of LCA Tejas MK I for Indian Air Force', 20 February 2019; 'Prime Minister & his Spanish counterpart jointly inaugurate TATA Aircraft Complex for manufacturing of C-295 aircraft in Vadodara', 28 October 2024; 'MoD inks two contracts worth Rs 62,700 crore with HAL for supply of 156 LCH, Prachand', 28 March 2025; News On AIR, 'Civil Aviation Minister expresses happiness over successful test flight of indigenous Airbus C295', 11 June 2026; consulted 14 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of a UAV and a UAS

An unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is an aircraft that flies without a pilot physically present on board. An unmanned aircraft system (UAS) includes the aircraft and the supporting elements needed to operate it, such as control equipment and communication links.

The familiar word drone is often used for a UAV or UAS. However, these expressions are not identical in every technical context. A UAV is the flying vehicle; a UAS is the wider system.

A remotely piloted aircraft system (RPAS) is a UAS in which a remote pilot controls the aircraft. Some other UAS can execute pre-programmed flight functions with varying degrees of automation.

Classification by aircraft configuration

Fixed-wing UAVs

Fixed-wing UAVs obtain lift primarily from their wings. They are suited to missions requiring sustained forward flight, such as surveying large areas. Most conventional fixed-wing UAVs cannot hover like a helicopter.

Rotary-wing UAVs

Rotary-wing UAVs use rotating blades to produce lift. A quadcopter is a multirotor UAV with 4 rotors. Such vehicles can hover, take off vertically and examine a relatively small area without requiring a runway. Their endurance and payload depend on their design and energy source.

Hybrid or vertical-take-off-and-landing UAVs

A hybrid UAV may combine vertical take-off or landing with efficient forward flight. Its configuration is intended to obtain advantages from more than one aircraft type. It does not automatically perform better than every fixed-wing or rotary-wing UAV.

Classification by mission

  • Surveillance and reconnaissance UAVs: Collect images or other observations to improve awareness of an area.
  • Mapping and survey UAVs: Collect data for maps, terrain inspection or infrastructure assessment.
  • Logistics UAVs: Move small supplies or other permitted cargo.
  • Combat UAVs: Are designed to undertake military combat tasks.
  • Loitering munitions: Are weapons that remain airborne while searching for or waiting for an authorised engagement opportunity. Unlike an ordinary reusable surveillance drone, the weapon is generally expended during its intended use.

A camera-equipped UAV is not necessarily a combat UAV. The presence of a sensor, a remote-control link or an autopilot does not by itself establish the aircraft's military role.

India's regulatory classification by maximum weight

The Drone Rules, 2021, issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, classify unmanned aircraft according to their maximum all-up weight, including payload. This is a civil regulatory weight classification, not a classification of their military combat role or endurance.

ClassMaximum all-up weight, including payload
NanoUp to and including 250 g
MicroMore than 250 g and up to 2 kg
SmallMore than 2 kg and up to 25 kg
MediumMore than 25 kg and up to 150 kg
LargeMore than 150 kg

The boundary values matter. A drone weighing exactly 250 g falls in the nano class; exactly 2 kg in the micro class; exactly 25 kg in the small class; and exactly 150 kg in the medium class.

Military endurance and operating-area terms

Military UAVs are also described according to their operating altitude, endurance and use. MALE means Medium-Altitude Long-Endurance, while HALE means High-Altitude Long-Endurance. These terms express an operating concept rather than the weight limits laid down in the Drone Rules, 2021. The exact altitude or endurance thresholds used by different organisations may vary.

A small reconnaissance drone, a long-endurance maritime surveillance UAV and a remotely operated combat UAV may all be unmanned aircraft, but they have different performance requirements and mission systems.

Prelims focus

  • UAV means unmanned aerial vehicle; UAS includes the aircraft and its supporting operating system.
  • A quadcopter is a rotary-wing or multirotor UAV with 4 rotors.
  • The Drone Rules, 2021, use maximum all-up weight including payload.
  • Nano is up to 250 g; micro is more than 250 g to 2 kg; small is more than 2 kg to 25 kg.
  • Medium is more than 25 kg to 150 kg; large exceeds 150 kg.
  • Trap: MALE and HALE describe altitude and endurance, not the nano-to-large civil weight classes.

[Sources: Ministry of Civil Aviation, Drone Rules, 2021, rule on classification of unmanned aircraft systems, notified 25 August 2021; Press Information Bureau Research Unit, 'The Drone Rules, 2021', 28 January 2022, section 'Classification of unmanned aircraft systems'; consulted 14 November 2026.]
